introduction: “This is the Day”: the phrase opens tablet after tablet of Bahá’u’lláh, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá repeats it to audiences in Paris, London and America as the “century of light”. The claim is that the present age is the one all the scriptures promised, greater than any before it, and that its signs are visible in the spread of the Cause, in science, in the shrinking of the world, and in the rise of women. A hundred of the guide’s three hundred quotations are given here, ten from each tenth of its length. Beside them stand a hundred voices from elsewhere: the prophets on the day of the Lord, the Gospels on what kings and prophets longed to see, the Qur’an’s Night of Power, Wordsworth’s dawn, Whitman, Tennyson, Hugo. About three in ten do not simply agree. Amos and Yeats fear the day; Dickens, Arnold and Hardy saw the same century differently; the Preacher doubts that any age is new. Those end in a question.
questions: Bahá’u’lláh says the excellence of this Day is beyond comprehension; Emerson says every time is a good one if we know what to do with it; the Preacher says nothing is new. What would it take to show that an age really is different?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá names science, communications and books among the signs of the century of light. Marx, Tennyson and the Preacher each ask what such progress costs or leaves undone. How do you weigh them a century on?
Amos warned those who longed for the day of the Lord, and Malachi asked who could abide it. Why do the readings, too, speak of terror as well as joy?
Wordsworth thought it bliss to be alive in 1789, and Hardy heard a hope he could not share in 1900. What do the readings ask of someone living in a time they call blessed?
Women’s boldness is called one of the miracles of this Dispensation. Set this beside Deborah, the women at the tomb, and Paul’s “neither male nor female”. What has changed, and what has not?
“A single minute of these days cannot be compared with the centuries of bygone ages.” Herrick and Kipling also say seize the time. What, in the readings, is the time to be seized for?

outside.why: “Oh, how I long to announce unto every spot on the surface of the earth … the glad-tidings of this Revelation.” Isaiah praised the very feet of one who brings such news.
Bahá’u’lláh quotes this verse of Isaiah and says no one who meditates on it can doubt the greatness of the Day of God. Here it is in full.

The verse from Isaiah is taken as proof of how exalted the Day is. Amos warned those who longed for it: the day of the Lord is darkness, and not light. Why would a prophet tell people not to wish for the very day they were waiting for?
“This is the Night in which … the portals leading unto the divine presence were … flung open.” The Qur’an has such a night: better than a thousand months, and peace until the rising of the dawn.
“A Night the world of creation hath never seen its like.” Luke’s shepherds, keeping watch by night, are told of good tidings of great joy.
The night has come “for the harvesting of the ages”. Jesus: lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest.
“The time preordained for this Revelation was fulfilled.” Paul’s phrase for the coming of Christ: when the fulness of the time was come.

“The excellence of this Day is immensely exalted above the comprehension of men.” Emerson told the students of Harvard that this time, like all times, is a very good one, if we but know what to do with it. Is one age really greater than another, or only better used?
A bounty such as nothing from the beginning to the end can rival. The Preacher: there is no new thing under the sun. What would he have needed to see to change his mind?
The day exceeds every measure of knowledge. The Psalmist’s answer to any day given by God is simpler: we will rejoice and be glad in it.
“The prestige of the Faith of God has immensely increased.” Gamaliel gave the council a rule for judging any such growth: if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it.
“These are the days which the people in bygone times eagerly expected.” Jesus said the same to his disciples: many prophets and righteous men have desired to see those things which ye see.
“A different Sun hath arisen, and a different Heaven … The world is another world.” Isaiah: behold, I create new heavens and a new earth.
The world is another world. The voice from the throne at the end of the Bible: behold, I make all things new.

The holy ones of the past longed to live a moment in this Day. Jesus says something as startling of John the Baptist: none greater was born of women, yet the least in the kingdom is greater than he. Is greatness here a matter of the person or of the time?
“All the Divine Books and Scriptures have predicted … the advent of the Most Great Revelation.” Haggai’s name for what is awaited: the desire of all nations.
“In this day the breeze of God is wafted, and His Spirit hath pervaded all things.” Joel: I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh.

The rivers of earlier revelation “are joined to this Most Great Ocean” and reach their consummation. The Preacher watched rivers too: all run into the sea, yet the sea is not full, and they return again. Is there such a thing as a final consummation?
“The Day on which all eyes shall stare up with terror.” Malachi: who may abide the day of his coming? for he is like a refiner’s fire.
The hearts of those on earth shall tremble. Zephaniah’s lines, which became the hymn Dies irae: a day of wrath, a day of trouble and distress.
“The five continents of the earth have virtually merged into one.” Whitman, on the Suez Canal and the Pacific railway: the earth to be spanned, connected by network, the lands to be welded together.
All the members of the human family “have become increasingly interdependent”. An American president half a century later: our most basic common link is that we all inhabit this small planet.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá welcomes the age of communication as the ground of unity. Marx saw the same forces at work and what they dissolved: all that is solid melts into air, all that is holy is profaned. What does the new closeness cost?
“America has developed powers and capacities greater and more wonderful than other nations.” The lines on the Statue of Liberty say what the country promised to be.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá hopes America will become “the distributing center of spiritual enlightenment”. Kipling, at the height of another nation’s power, warned it: all our pomp of yesterday is one with Nineveh and Tyre. What keeps a favoured nation from that end?
“In every century a particular and central theme is … confirmed by God.” The Preacher: to every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose.
“Every era hath a spirit.” Lowell, in the anti-slavery struggle: new occasions teach new duties; time makes ancient good uncouth.

“Thank ye God that ye have come into the plane of existence in this radiant century.” Wordsworth felt it in 1789: bliss was it in that dawn to be alive. He lived to see the Terror. How does one tell a true dawn?
A radiant century, the doors of the Kingdom open. Dickens on an earlier age that thought as well of itself: it was the best of times, it was the worst of times. Can both be said of ours?
“The renown of His Cause hath reached to east and west.” Habakkuk: the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea.
This day stands “at the summit of all days” for its sciences and arts. Tennyson, in the same century: knowledge comes, but wisdom lingers. Are sciences and arts the measure of a day?
The light of truth “has heretofore been seen dimly through variegated glasses”. Paul: now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face.
Variegated glasses, and then translucent mirrors. Shelley: life, like a dome of many-coloured glass, stains the white radiance of eternity.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá counts the books of this era against those of a hundred ages as proof of its greatness. The Preacher: of making many books there is no end, and much study is a weariness of the flesh. Is more written the same as more known?
“The tidings of the world’s Great Peace have created tumult in the realm of the hearts.” Victor Hugo told a peace congress in 1849 that a day would come, and described it.

Love has spread in East and West and the Great Peace is announced. Yeats, just after the Great War, expected another kind of advent: what rough beast, its hour come round at last? Which reading of the century has the evidence?
The tabernacle of fellowship is raised in the heart of the world. Tennyson dreamed it in 1842: the Parliament of man, the Federation of the world.
In this Dispensation “some handmaidens arose who excelled men in the arena of knowledge”. Tennyson: the woman’s cause is man’s; they rise or sink together.
Women’s achievements are counted among the signs of the age. In 1848, the year of the Báb’s followers’ gathering at Badasht, American women declared that all men and women are created equal.
“In the beginning, how small is the seed, yet in the end it is a mighty tree.” Jesus’ parable of the kingdom.
After Christ’s small band became a great tree, “now shall come to pass even greater things than these”. Jesus had promised his own followers the like: greater works than these shall he do.
In this cycle women “will become the envy of men”, a pattern for heroes. Deborah told Barak the honour of his battle would go to a woman.
The Qur’an sets women beside men, phrase by phrase, in everything it asks and everything it promises.

Science has so advanced that all call this the “Century of Light”, and the talk counts it a spiritual sign. Bacon thought a little science inclines to atheism and depth brings the mind back. Which has the century’s science done?
The learned call it the Century of Light. Kant had said what makes an age enlightened: the courage to use one’s own understanding.

Bahá’u’lláh “has brought the force to rend the veils” and given the age its soul. Arnold, in 1855, felt himself wandering between two worlds, one dead, the other powerless to be born. What does his century look like from where he stood?
Never before had someone from the East travelled to the far West to speak in its churches and halls. Kipling’s ballad: there is neither East nor West when two strong men stand face to face.
Why should this Cause “be regarded as impossible of achievement?” Micah set down the same improbable hope: nation shall not lift up a sword against nation, and none shall make them afraid.
Women “have evinced a greater boldness than men” in this Faith. On Easter morning it was women who brought the news, and their words seemed to the apostles as idle tales.

Women’s boldness is counted among the miracles of this Dispensation. Paul wrote that in Christ there is neither male nor female, and his churches kept women silent for centuries. How long can a principle wait for its practice?
“Seize, O friends, the chance which this Day offereth you.” Paul: behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation.
“So great is the glory of the Cause of God that even the blind can perceive it.” The man born blind, pressed by his examiners: one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see.
Even the blind. Isaiah’s sign of the promised day: then the eyes of the blind shall be opened.
“Everything that can be seen is a witness, and calleth all men unto the one true God.” The Psalm: the heavens declare the glory of God.
Every visible thing a witness. The Qur’an: We shall show them Our portents on the horizons and within themselves.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá tells Christians that “the promises of nineteen hundred years ago are today fulfilled”. The promise as John wrote it down.

The Son of Man is here in the Kingdom of His Father, and its doors are open. Jesus once answered those who asked when the kingdom would come: it cometh not with observation; it is within you. Does a kingdom arrive at a date?
“Do you appreciate the Day in which you live?” Thoreau ends Walden on the condition: only that day dawns to which we are awake. How much of a day’s greatness depends on the one living in it?
“This is the consummate day of all the Prophets!” Hebrews opens with the same sense of arrival: God, who spoke in time past by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken.
Were the greatness of this Day revealed in full, “most men would swoon away”. Moses is told the same of God’s glory: there shall no man see me, and live.
“A Revelation that infuseth strength into the feeble, and crowneth with wealth the destitute.” Mary’s song: he hath exalted them of low degree; he hath filled the hungry with good things.
Strength for the feeble. Isaiah: he giveth power to the faint; they shall mount up with wings as eagles.
“Seize ye the opportunity in My days.” Herrick says seize the day too, and means roses and youth: gather ye rosebuds while ye may. What separates the two kinds of urgency?
“All must regard the time as precious.” Paul: walk circumspectly, redeeming the time.
A single minute of these days outweighs centuries. Kipling’s test of a man: to fill the unforgiving minute with sixty seconds’ worth of distance run.
“The traces of every soul that ariseth today shall remain on earth”; all else will vanish. Shelley’s traveller found what remained of a king of kings. What kind of trace lasts?
“This Day has no equal. In this transient station, one must acquire an everlasting rank.” The Psalm: so teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
“We created the world for this Most Great Day, yet when it appeared, the divines of the earth denied it.” John’s Gospel: he came unto his own, and his own received him not.
“If the people but knew, they would have circumambulated His Throne.” Jesus, weeping over Jerusalem: thou knewest not the time of thy visitation.

Souls in the past longed for this radiant century. Hardy dated a poem to the last evening of the nineteenth, in a dead landscape, and heard a thrush sing of “some blessed Hope” he was unaware of. What did the century look like to those who lived through it?
“It is a blessed century; it is a blessed day.” Tennyson’s New Year bells: ring out the old, ring in the new; ring out the false, ring in the true.
From within a prison Bahá’u’lláh “revealed and advanced such a sublime Revelation”. Paul, in chains: the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel.
A Revelation spread from a prison cell. Lovelace, in a London gaol: stone walls do not a prison make, nor iron bars a cage.
The Cause appeared in Persia, “yet until now its people remain heedless of it”. Jesus over his own city: thou that killest the prophets, how often would I have gathered thy children.
The Hijaz, “deserted and sterile”, was made the centre of the world’s devotion. Isaiah: the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose.
An ignorant people in a barren land. Paul on how God chooses: the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, the weak to confound the mighty.
“All things have been stirred by its most sweet call.” The complaint made against Paul’s companions in Thessalonica: these that have turned the world upside down are come hither also.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá says the Great War “caused all the divine texts to be fulfilled”. Wilfred Owen, who died in it, asked what passing-bells there were for those who die as cattle. Can a fulfilled prophecy be good news to the people it happens to?
“Erelong the power of the Kingdom will encompass all the world.” The Qur’an’s chapter for the hour of victory: then hymn the praises of thy Lord, and seek forgiveness.
The unfaithful strive “to extinguish His radiant Light”. The Qur’an: fain would they put out the light of God with their mouths, but God will perfect His light.
“No power on earth can stand in the path of the progress of the Bahá’í Cause.” Machiavelli’s rule of history was that unarmed prophets are destroyed. What would count as his being wrong?
No power can stand in its path. Zechariah names the kind of power meant: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.

Governors and generals humbly sought the presence of a prisoner, and were seldom admitted. Mencius describes the great man whom riches and power cannot move. What gives one person that standing with those who hold force?

The Cause “hath never been so plain and evident as in this most great Cycle”. Abraham in the parable says that those who do not hear Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded though one rose from the dead. Does plainness of evidence settle anything?
“This is the Day that hath been mentioned and recorded in all the Books.” Jesus to those who could read the sky: can ye not discern the signs of the times?
The Revelation is “the Purpose and Promise of all the Prophets of God”. Daniel’s form of the promise: a kingdom which shall never be destroyed.
“All creation hath been set in motion, and the universe vibrateth with tidings of joy.” The Psalm calls on sun, moon and stars to praise.
“Every atom in existence is ecstatic with delight.” The Qur’an: there is not a thing but hymneth His praise.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá hears every atom rejoicing in this Age. Tennyson, a few decades earlier, heard Nature shriek against the creed that love is creation’s law. Is the joy in the creation or in the hearer?
“This is the time for gladness, the day of joy and exhilaration.” The Song of Solomon: the winter is past, the time of the singing of birds is come.
Were all the writers of the earth to describe this Day, “they would surely find themselves powerless”. John ends his Gospel in the same way: the world itself could not contain the books.
No pen can describe it. The Qur’an: though the sea became ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be used up first.
In this Day God has manifested “that which was hidden in Thy Knowledge”. Moses: the secret things belong unto the Lord; those which are revealed belong unto us.
“The call of Thy Greatest Name hath caused a mighty reverberation throughout all the kingdoms.” Paul quotes the Psalm for his own mission: their sound went into all the earth.
The Day “all the Prophets and Messengers … yearned after”. Jesus marks the same turning: the law and the prophets were until John; since that time the kingdom of God is preached.

This Day stands “unequalled amongst all the days of Thy world”. The Preacher rebukes the opposite opinion: say not thou that the former days were better than these. Why do people so readily think the best days are behind them, or ahead?
“Behold, how firm and strong is the foundation of the Cause of God.” Jesus’ house built on rock: the floods came and the winds blew, and it fell not.
The Day on which God shed “the splendor of the glory of all Thy names upon all created things”. The Qur’an: and the earth shineth with the light of her Lord.
The colours of the world are evanescent to anyone with eyes. Prospero: the cloud-capped towers, the gorgeous palaces, shall dissolve, and leave not a rack behind.

“A new life is, in this age, stirring within all the peoples of the earth.” Shelley’s chorus says so, and then doubts: the world’s great age begins anew … O cease! must hate and death return? What would keep the new life from going the way of earlier dawns?

psalm-day-which-the-lord-hath-made.text: This is the day which the Lord hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it

luke-good-tidings-of-great-joy.text: And there were in the same country shepherds abiding in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night. And, lo, the angel of the Lord came upon them, and the glory of the Lord shone round about them: and they were sore afraid. And the angel said unto them, Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord

corinthians-now-is-the-accepted-time.text: For he saith, I have heard thee in a time accepted, and in the day of salvation

galatians-fulness-of-the-time.text: But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, To redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons

amos-woe-unto-you-that-desire.text: Woe unto you that desire the day of the Lord! to what end is it for you? the day of the Lord is darkness, and not light. As if a man did flee from a lion, and a bear met him; or went into the house, and leaned his hand on the wall, and a serpent bit him. Shall not the day of the Lord be darkness, and not light? even very dark, and no brightness in it

malachi-who-may-abide.text: But who may abide the day of his coming? and who shall stand when he appeareth? for he is like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap

john-white-already-to-harvest.text: Say not ye, There are yet four months, and then cometh harvest? behold, I say unto you, Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest

ephesians-redeeming-the-time.text: See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, Redeeming the time, because the days are evil

luke-idle-tales.text: It was Mary Magdalene and Joanna, and Mary the mother of James, and other women that were with them, which told these things unto the apostles. And their words seemed to them as idle tales, and they believed them not

zephaniah-great-day-of-the-lord.text: The great day of the Lord is near, it is near, and hasteth greatly, even the voice of the day of the Lord: the mighty man shall cry there bitterly. That day is a day of wrath, a day of trouble and distress, a day of wasteness and desolation, a day of darkness and gloominess, a day of clouds and thick darkness

isaiah-giveth-power-to-the-faint.text: He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength. Even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall: But they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint

judges-hand-of-a-woman.text: And Barak said unto her, If thou wilt go with me, then I will go: but if thou wilt not go with me, then I will not go. And she said, I will surely go with thee: notwithstanding the journey that thou takest shall not be for thine honour; for the Lord shall sell Sisera into the hand of a woman

quran-earth-shineth.text: And the earth shineth with the light of her Lord, and the Book is set up, and the prophets and the witnesses are brought, and it is judged between them with truth, and they are not wronged.

quran-men-and-women-who-surrender.text: Lo! men who surrender unto Allah, and women who surrender, and men who believe and women who believe, and men who obey and women who obey, and men who speak the truth and women who speak the truth, and men who persevere (in righteousness) and women who persevere, and men who are humble and women who are humble, and men who give alms and women who give alms, and men who fast and women who fast, and men who guard their modesty and women who guard (their modesty), and men who remember Allah much and women who remember - Allah hath prepared for them forgiveness and a vast reward.

quran-succour-and-triumph.text: When Allah's succour and the triumph cometh And thou seest mankind entering the religion of Allah in troops, Then hymn the praises of thy Lord, and seek forgiveness of Him. Lo! He is ever ready to show mercy

wordsworth-bliss-in-that-dawn.text: Bliss was it in that dawn to be alive, / But to be young was very heaven
wordsworth-bliss-in-that-dawn.author: William Wordsworth
wordsworth-bliss-in-that-dawn.work: French Revolution, as It Appeared to Enthusiasts at Its Commencement

emerson-this-time-like-all-times.text: This time, like all times, is a very good one, if we but know what to do with it
emerson-this-time-like-all-times.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

lazarus-golden-door.text: Give me your tired, your poor, / Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free, / The wretched refuse of your teeming shore. / Send these, the homeless, tempest-tost to me, / I lift my lamp beside the golden door
lazarus-golden-door.author: Emma Lazarus

kipling-recessional.text: Far-called, our navies melt away; / On dune and headland sinks the fire: / Lo, all our pomp of yesterday / Is one with Nineveh and Tyre! / Judge of the Nations, spare us yet, / Lest we forget
kipling-recessional.author: Rudyard Kipling

arnold-between-two-worlds.text: Wandering between two worlds, one dead, / The other powerless to be born
arnold-between-two-worlds.author: Matthew Arnold

yeats-rough-beast.text: And what rough beast, its hour come round at last, / Slouches towards Bethlehem to be born
yeats-rough-beast.author: W. B. Yeats

whitman-earth-to-be-spanned.text: Lo, soul, seest thou not God's purpose from the first? / The earth to be spann'd, connected by network, / The races, neighbors, to marry and be given in marriage, / The oceans to be cross'd, the distant brought near, / The lands to be welded together
whitman-earth-to-be-spanned.author: Walt Whitman

marx-all-that-is-solid.text: All that is solid melts into air, all that is holy is profaned, and man is at last compelled to face with sober senses, his real conditions of life, and his relations with his kind
marx-all-that-is-solid.author: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels

dickens-best-of-times.text: It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness, it was the epoch of belief, it was the epoch of incredulity, it was the season of Light, it was the season of Darkness, it was the spring of hope, it was the winter of despair
dickens-best-of-times.author: Charles Dickens
